title: Warp and weft
hook: Kabir pictures the world as cloth on the Lord's loom, and the body as the place the weaver comes home

segments.voice: Yesterday, julaha: Kabir called himself a weaver, and sang his devotion at the level of the thread, a weaver's song. Today the whole universe goes on his loom.

Pull a thread from the hem of your sleeve and you'll find it isn't alone. Every piece of cloth is two sets of thread. One is stretched long and tight on the loom before anything begins: that's the warp. The other runs across it, over and under, carried by the shuttle: that's the weft. Neither one is cloth by itself. Only crossed do they hold. Kabir knew this the way a cook knows salt. And in one hymn he takes the whole loom, frame and thread and shuttle, and hangs the universe on it.
screen: `TWO SETS OF THREAD.` → `THE WARP, STRETCHED LONG.` → `THE WEFT, CARRIED ACROSS.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Asa, and it begins with a riddle. Nobody, Kabir says, knows the secret of the Weaver, who has stretched out the whole world as his warp. God here is not a king on a throne. God is a weaver, and the world is the long thread on the frame. Then it widens. The earth and the sky are made into the loom. The sun and the moon move across together, like the shuttles going back and forth. You can almost hear it: day, night, day, night, the weft running across the warp. There's even a little jab in it. While you sat listening to the Vedas and the Puranas, he says, I stretched out this much of my warp. I was working, and the work was teaching me. Then the hymn turns inward. The weaver, Kabir sings, came to know his own home, and recognized the Lord right inside the body. The loom outside became the loom within. And it ends at the end of a life. When the loom is broken, he says, the weaver merges thread into thread. The cloth comes off the frame, and the thread goes back to the thread it came from. Some readers hear in this the soul returning to the One it was always part of. Nothing in the picture is wasted, and nothing is separate: crossed, over and under, until it holds.
screen: `NOBODY KNOWS THE WEAVER'S SECRET.` · `EARTH AND SKY, THE LOOM.` · `THE LORD, INSIDE THE BODY.` · `THREAD MERGES INTO THREAD.` · then, large: `WOVEN.`

segments.voice: Bring a piece of cloth close to your eyes, a sleeve, a towel, the knee of your jeans, and find the threads running one way, then the threads crossing them. Follow one thread as far as you can before it slips under another, and notice that it never stops being itself, and never stops holding the others. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly as you trace it.
Weaver. Kabir's name for the Lord, who stretches out the whole world as warp, with the sun and moon crossing it like shuttles.
Your line: woven. A week that closed the sakhis and opened the bhagats, crossed and held. Seven hundred forty-nine days, and counting.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing and reflect on Kabir's loom hymns in kirtan and katha, reading the weaver and the cloth as pictures of the Creator, the world and the soul.

fork.setup: you're Kabir, a weaver, and others sit listening to learned texts. you want to sing about God and the world. what picture do you reach for?

what it means: in Kabir's hymn the world is the Lord's warp, and day and night run across it like weft.
what a scholar hears: the hymn ends with the broken loom and thread merging into thread, which many readers hear as the soul returning to the One.

chat.says: Kabir has a hymn about a loom. Who's the weaver in it?
options: The Lord: the world is the warp, and the sun and moon cross it like shuttles.
Kabir himself; it's a song about his day job, not really about God at all.
The king of Kashi, who owned the looms that Kabir and his family worked.
chat.meaning: In Raag Asa, nobody knows the Weaver's secret: the world is His warp, earth and sky the loom, the sun and moon the shuttles.

warp.meaning: the threads stretched long and tight on a loom

weft.meaning: the threads carried across the warp by the shuttle

Raag Asa.meaning: one of the musical modes the Granth's hymns are set in

Vedas.meaning: the old hymns of the Hindu tradition

Puranas.meaning: old Hindu books of sacred story

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Asa, Kabir, Ang 484 (the Weaver's secret; earth and sky the loom; sun and moon; the broken loom)

notes: All of the Asa hymn is paraphrased (Ang 484, the hymn on the 'kori' and the 'taana'). Confirm Ang, and that 'sun and moon move across together, like the shuttles' fairly renders the line about the moon and sun.
'Sikh readers hear in this the soul returning to the One' is an interpretive gloss; confirm.

The hymn's sharp line about listening to the Vedas and Puranas is softened to 'a little jab'; confirm it isn't read as dismissing those texts (day 753 covers Kabir's 'don't call the scriptures false').
